title: Microburst backpressure emulation + KV warmup simulation — field notes
content:
Summary:

This doc captures experiments from Jan 2026 that emulate client-side microbursts and soft backpressure through proxies, and observes the knock-on effects on KV-cache warmup and tail latency. The goal: understand how short, high-concurrency spikes interact with proxy buffering and streaming chunk patterns to produce p95/p99 latency regressions and cache-cold amplification across requests.

Motivation / why this matters:
- Real traffic: PLG customers sometimes generate microbursts (hundreds of concurrent short requests) from UI-driven autoscaling and bulk request windows.
- Observed symptom: intermittent p99 latency spikes and step-changes in downstream token-generation latency correlated with proxy memory pressure and KV cache miss storms.
- Hypothesis: proxy buffering + client chunk behavior creates short-term head-of-line effects; cached KV-values for recent prefixes are evicted or unavailable during bursts resulting in cache-warmup cascades.

Hypotheses tested:
1) Larger proxy response buffers (Envoy) reduce connection-level backpressure and increase server concurrency, which amplifies KV-cache cold windows and raises p99.
2) Coarse-grained chunking (large chunks with long inter-chunk delays) interacts poorly with proxy buffering: buffers hold entire responses, preventing incremental flush and delaying downstream consumers.
3) Client-side pacing (micro-delay between request starts) can smooth cache warmups and reduce p99 more cost-effectively than increasing infra.

Experiment environment:
- Hardware: Dedicated cluster (c5n clients, p4d inference nodes running CUDA 11.8).
- Runtime: serving-runtime branch feature/streaming-proxy-experiments (PR linked above).
- Proxy: Envoy 1.26 sidecar; two configurations: small-buffer (10KB per-stream), large-buffer (2MB per-stream).
- Models: Llama-2-style 7B-like model (quantized) with KV-cache enabled. Token generation ~12 ms/token cold, ~3 ms/token hot (approx).
- Workload generator: custom gRPC streaming client (python, asyncio) that can emit bursts: N concurrent streams, each sending a streaming request, and optionally chunking the prompt in M chunks with inter-chunk delay d ms. Also used ghz for non-streaming baselines.
- Key metrics collected: per-request total latency, per-chunk latency, buffer-occupancy (envoy stats), server queue_depth, kv_cache_hit_rate, p50/p95/p99 latencies, tokens/s.

Experiment matrix (selected):
- Burst sizes: 50, 200, 800 concurrent streams for 3s windows every 30s (to emulate UI spikes).
- Chunk strategies: (A) monolithic single chunk (<=64KB), (B) 16KB chunks @ 10ms gap, (C) 2KB chunks @ 2ms gap.
- Proxy buffer: small vs large.
- Client pacing: none (all start concurrently) vs staggered 5–20ms jitter.

Representative commands / test harness notes:
- python loadgen/grpc_stream_burst.py --concurrency 200 --burst-duration 3 --burst-interval 30 --chunks 4 --chunk-size 16384 --inter-chunk-ms 10 --pacing 0
- Envoy config knobs changed: per_stream_buffer_limit_bytes, drain_timeout, http2_initial_stream_window_size.

Key observations (numeric):
- Baseline (no burst): p50=85ms, p95=210ms, p99=380ms (single chunk strategy, small-buffer). KV hit rate steady ~92%.
- Large burst (800 conc), large-buffer, monolithic chunk: p50=120ms (+41%), p95=610ms (+190%), p99=1300ms (+242%). KV hit rate dropped to ~45% during burst window; observed cache miss cascade where many requests needed full re-computation.
- Same burst, small-buffer, fine-grained chunks (2KB@2ms): p50=95ms, p95=260ms, p99=470ms. KV hit rate ~78%.
- With client pacing (staggering 5–15ms) and small-buffer+fine chunks: p95 reduced by ~22% vs unpaced small-buffer case, p99 reduced by ~35%.
- Envoy buffer occupancy graph (sample): large-buffer config showed sustained per-stream allocations of ~1.8MB during bursts; backlog on server queue_depth rose 3–4x. Small-buffer limited per-stream memory and forced earlier backpressure onto clients, which paradoxically improved server-side KV hit rate because fewer concurrent in-flight token generation sessions were active.

Interpretation / root cause analysis:
- Large per-stream buffers in the proxy mask streaming behavior. When buffers absorb streamed bytes, the server sees steady read progress and continues to accept new work, leading to more concurrent token generation. This increases working set size for the KV cache and causes effective eviction/pressure, increasing cache misses. The runtime's KvCache is sized for typical concurrency; microbursts exceed that transiently.
- Coarse chunking compounds the issue: one large chunk holds many tokens in the proxy and delays the ability to interleave cancellation or backpressure signals. Fine-grained chunks allow more immediate propagation of partial responses and early client-side consumption, which helps throughput/latency and reduces concurrency pressure on token generators.
- Client-side pacing is an effective mitigation: smoothing request arrival reduces peak concurrent token generators and lets KV caches remain hot across bursts.

Practical recommendations (short to medium term):
1) Default Envoy per_stream_buffer_limit_bytes -> 32KB (from current 2MB) for streaming endpoints. Rationale: avoids opaque buffering that increases server concurrency and cache pressure.
2) Encourage fine-grained chunking in SDK: default chunk size 4KB with 1–5ms inter-chunk gap for browser SDKs. Add an advanced flag for low-latency heavy-throughput workloads.
3) Add client-side jitter/pacing snippets to SDK quickstarts and sample apps.
4) Expose runtime KV-cache occupancy metrics and eviction_rate as first-class metrics in Console (per-model, per-node).
5) Add a traffic-shaping policy at edge: when queue_depth > threshold, slow-accept new requests (reject 429 or inject small start-delay).

Telemetry & dashboards to build:
- Per-stream buffer bytes (Envoy), histogram of buffer duration over threshold.
- KV cache hit-rate heatmap by request arrival time; correlate with queue_depth.
- Per-chunk latency histogram (to check chunk flush patterns).
- P95/P99 correlated with concurrent_token_generators metric.

Open questions / items for follow-up/test: 
- How do these results change with larger models (Llama-70B) where token generation cost is higher? My hypothesis: cache pressure effect will be amplified because cold tokens are much slower—need to re-run with a slower token generator to measure absolute p99.
- Can we implement an adaptive per-stream buffer size that drops to small-buffer when queue_depth crosses a threshold? Is that doable in Envoy without custom filter?
- Explore the interaction with HTTP/2 SETTINGS (initial window size). In some runs larger initial windows allowed upstream to pump more data before client read; need targeted experiments.

Quick todo list (owners):
- (Asha) Create PR to change envoy default per_stream_buffer_limit_bytes for streaming routes and measure 24h in staging (ENG-1298).
- (Liam) Add KV-cache eviction_rate metric and wire to Console; include alert if eviction_rate spikes > 10% in 1m.
- (Priya) Draft SDK chunking recommendation doc and patch browser SDK sample (small chunk + jitter).
- (Marco) Run a slower-model (simulated token gen 3x baseline) matrix and post results to Confluence.

Notes to reviewers:
- These are field notes from emulations rather than production traces. We tried to model production-like microburst shapes based on telemetry but there will be variation in real customer traffic.
- Config changes to proxies must be rolled out carefully: lowering buffers could increase apparent client-side latency for some mobile clients with poor connectivity; propose staged rollout behind feature flag.

Attachments / artifacts collected (bench logs):
- raw latency histograms (gzipped) uploaded to S3: s3://redwood-tests/microburst/2026-01-12/
- envoy stats dumps and runbook snippet in the linked PR above.

Closing thought:
- The main takeaway: buffering hides backpressure and pushes pressure inside the serving runtime where caches and computational limits are. Smoothing traffic (client pacing + smaller chunks) and making proxy behavior less opaque yields lower p99 for most microburst scenarios without adding hardware.

-- Asha
